description: Symbolic algebra in the Wolfram Language centers on transforming expressions into equivalent forms: expanding and factoring, putting rational expressions over a common denominator, extracting polynomial data, and simplifying under assumptions. This category covers those transformations together with the trigonometric and complex-expansion functions and the assumption machinery that controls them.

tools.name: Expand
tools.description: Multiplies out products and positive integer powers in the top level of an expression, leaving denominators and function arguments alone. Expand[expr, patt] expands only the terms containing something matching patt, which keeps large expressions manageable. Use ExpandAll to expand everywhere, including inside denominators and nested functions.
tools.usage:
Expand[expr]
Expand[expr, patt]
Expand[expr, Modulus -> p]
tools.example:
Expand[(x + 1)^3]
Expand[(a + b) (c + d)]
Expand[(x + y)^2 + (u + v)^2, x]
Expand[(1 + x)^5, Modulus -> 2]
tools.notes: Expand does not touch denominators; use ExpandAll, or Together followed by Expand on the numerator, for rational expressions.

tools.name: ExpandAll
tools.description: Expands products and powers everywhere in an expression, including inside numerators, denominators and the arguments of functions. It is the aggressive version of Expand and can make expressions much larger. A pattern argument restricts it to parts containing a given subexpression.
tools.example:
ExpandAll[(x + 1)^2 / (x - 1)^2]
ExpandAll[Sin[(a + b)^2]]
Expand[(x + 1)^2 / (x - 1)^2]

tools.name: Factor
tools.description: Factors a polynomial into irreducible factors over the rationals by default. Extension -> {r} allows algebraic number coefficients, GaussianIntegers -> True factors over the Gaussian integers, and Modulus -> p factors over a finite field. Factor also factors the numerator and denominator of a rational expression.
tools.usage:
Factor[poly]
Factor[poly, Modulus -> p]
Factor[poly, Extension -> {a}]
Factor[poly, GaussianIntegers -> True]
tools.example:
Factor[x^2 - 1]
Factor[x^4 - 1]
Factor[x^2 + 1, GaussianIntegers -> True]
Factor[x^2 - 2, Extension -> Sqrt[2]]
Factor[x^2 + x + 1, Modulus -> 3]
tools.notes: For integers use FactorInteger. Factor can be slow on high-degree multivariate polynomials; FactorList returns the factors with multiplicities in structured form.

tools.name: FactorList
tools.description: Gives the factors of a polynomial as a list of {factor, exponent} pairs, including the overall numeric content as the first entry. This structured form is much easier to process programmatically than the product returned by Factor. The same options as Factor control the coefficient domain.
tools.example:
FactorList[x^4 - 1]
FactorList[2 x^2 + 4 x + 2]
First /@ Rest[FactorList[x^3 - x]]
FactorList[x^2 + 1, GaussianIntegers -> True]

tools.name: Simplify
tools.description: Applies a broad set of algebraic and trigonometric transformations and returns the form with the smallest complexity measure. A second argument supplies assumptions such as x > 0 or n ∈ Integers, which unlock simplifications that are not valid in general. The ComplexityFunction and TimeConstraint options control what counts as simpler and how long to search.
tools.usage:
Simplify[expr]
Simplify[expr, assum]
Simplify[expr, assum, ComplexityFunction -> f]

parameters.name: assum
parameters.description: Assumptions about symbols, e.g. x > 0, n \[Element] Integers, or a list of such conditions.

parameters.name: TimeConstraint
parameters.description: Seconds to spend on each transformation attempt (default 300 for FullSimplify, shorter for Simplify).

tools.example:
Simplify[Sin[x]^2 + Cos[x]^2]
Simplify[Sqrt[x^2], x > 0]
Simplify[(x^2 - 1)/(x - 1)]
Simplify[Sin[n Pi], n \[Element] Integers]
tools.notes: Simplify uses a limited set of transformations for speed; FullSimplify tries many more. Neither is guaranteed to find the simplest form.

tools.name: FullSimplify
tools.description: Like Simplify but applies a much wider range of transformations, including identities for special functions, hypergeometric and elliptic functions and number-theoretic relations. It is correspondingly slower, so it is used when Simplify does not succeed. TransformationFunctions lets you supply additional custom rewriting rules.
tools.usage:
FullSimplify[expr]
FullSimplify[expr, assum]
FullSimplify[expr, assum, TransformationFunctions -> {...}]
tools.example:
FullSimplify[Gamma[n + 1]/Gamma[n], n > 0]
FullSimplify[Sqrt[6 + Sqrt[11]] - Sqrt[6 - Sqrt[11]]]
FullSimplify[BesselJ[1/2, x]]
FullSimplify[expr, TimeConstraint -> 60]
tools.notes: Set TimeConstraint to bound the search on large expressions. FullSimplify may return a different but equally valid form rather than the one you expect.

tools.name: Together
tools.description: Combines a sum of fractions into a single fraction over a common denominator and cancels common factors. It is the standard first step before Numerator, Denominator or Solve on a rational equation. The Modulus option performs the operation over a finite field.
tools.example:
Together[1/x + 1/y]
Together[1/(x - 1) + 1/(x + 1)]
Numerator[Together[a/b + c/d]]
Together[(x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) + 1]
tools.notes: Apart is the inverse operation, splitting a single fraction into partial fractions; Cancel only removes common factors without combining terms.

tools.name: Apart
tools.description: Rewrites a rational expression as a sum of terms with minimal denominators, i.e. the partial fraction decomposition. Apart[expr, var] treats only the named variable as the polynomial variable, which matters for multivariate expressions. It is the standard preparation for integrating or inverse-Laplace-transforming a rational function by hand.
tools.usage:
Apart[expr]
Apart[expr, var]
Apart[expr, Modulus -> p]
tools.example:
Apart[1/(x^2 - 1)]
Apart[(x + 2)/(x^2 + 3 x + 2)]
Apart[(a x + b)/(x (x + 1)), x]
Integrate[Apart[1/(x^2 - 1)], x]

tools.name: Cancel
tools.description: Cancels common factors between numerator and denominator of a rational expression without otherwise rearranging it. Unlike Together it does not combine separate fractions, and unlike Simplify it performs only this one operation, which makes it fast and predictable. It is the safe way to remove a known removable singularity.
tools.example:
Cancel[(x^2 - 1)/(x - 1)]
Cancel[(x^2 + 2 x)/(x^3)]
Cancel[a b / (b c)]
Together[Cancel[expr]]

tools.name: Collect
tools.description: Groups terms by powers of one or more variables, producing a polynomial arranged by those variables with the remaining coefficients gathered together. A third argument applies a function such as Simplify or Factor to each coefficient. It is the way to present a result in terms of the variable that matters.
tools.usage:
Collect[expr, var]
Collect[expr, {v1, v2, ...}]
Collect[expr, var, f]
tools.example:
Collect[a x + b x + c, x]
Collect[(x + y)^3, x]
Collect[a x^2 + b x^2 + c x, x, Simplify]
Collect[expr, {x, y}, Factor]
tools.notes: Collect only groups by the variables you name, leaving everything else in the coefficients; CoefficientList gives the coefficients as a plain array.

tools.name: Coefficient
tools.description: Extracts the coefficient of a particular power of a variable in a polynomial. Coefficient[expr, x] gives the coefficient of x^1 and Coefficient[expr, x, 0] gives the terms free of x. It also works with a monomial such as x y as the second argument.
tools.example:
Coefficient[3 x^2 + 5 x + 7, x]
Coefficient[3 x^2 + 5 x + 7, x, 2]
Coefficient[3 x^2 + 5 x + 7, x, 0]
Coefficient[a x y + b x, x y]
tools.notes: Coefficient[expr, x, 0] is not the same as expr /. x -> 0 when the expression has negative powers or non-polynomial structure.

tools.name: CoefficientList
tools.description: Gives the coefficients of a polynomial as a list indexed by power, starting with the constant term. For several variables it returns a nested array indexed by the multi-degree. It is the standard conversion from a symbolic polynomial to numeric coefficient data for further computation.
tools.example:
CoefficientList[1 + 2 x + 3 x^3, x]
CoefficientList[(1 + x)^4, x]
CoefficientList[x y + x^2, {x, y}]
FromDigits[Reverse[CoefficientList[p, x]], 10]
tools.notes: The list has length Exponent[poly, x] + 1 with explicit zeros for missing powers, so it maps directly onto array-based polynomial algorithms.

tools.name: Exponent
tools.description: Gives the highest power of a variable that appears in an expression, i.e. the degree. Exponent[expr, x, Min] gives the lowest power and Exponent[expr, x, List] gives all the exponents present. It works for negative and symbolic exponents as well as polynomials.
tools.example:
Exponent[x^3 + 2 x, x]
Exponent[1/x^2 + x, x, Min]
Exponent[x^2 + x^5, x, List]
Exponent[(1 + x)^10, x]

tools.name: Variables
tools.description: Gives the sorted list of independent variables appearing in a polynomial or rational expression. Symbolic subexpressions such as Sin[x] are treated as single variables when they are not polynomial in form. It is how you discover programmatically what a user-supplied expression depends on.
tools.example:
Variables[x^2 + y z]
Variables[a x^2 + b x + c]
Variables[Sin[t] + u]
Solve[expr == 0, Variables[expr]]
tools.notes: For a general expression, Cases[expr, _Symbol, Infinity] with DeleteDuplicates finds all symbols including constants; Variables is polynomial-aware.

tools.name: PolynomialQ
tools.description: Tests whether an expression is a polynomial in the given variable or variables, returning True or False. Without a variable argument it tests whether the expression is polynomial in all of its variables. Use it as an argument guard before calling polynomial-specific functions.
tools.example:
PolynomialQ[x^2 + 1, x]
PolynomialQ[1/x, x]
PolynomialQ[Sin[x], x]
PolynomialQ[x^2 y + y, {x, y}]

tools.name: PolynomialQuotient
tools.description: Gives the quotient of polynomial division of p by q with respect to a variable, discarding the remainder. Together with PolynomialRemainder it implements the division algorithm; PolynomialQuotientRemainder returns both at once. The Modulus option performs the division over a finite field.
tools.usage:
PolynomialQuotient[p, q, x]
PolynomialQuotient[p, q, x, Modulus -> n]
tools.example:
PolynomialQuotient[x^3 - 1, x - 1, x]
PolynomialQuotient[x^2 + 3 x + 2, x + 1, x]
PolynomialQuotientRemainder[x^3 + 1, x + 2, x]

tools.name: PolynomialRemainder
tools.description: Gives the remainder left after dividing one polynomial by another in a specified variable. It is the polynomial analogue of Mod and the basis of the Euclidean algorithm for polynomials. A zero remainder means q divides p exactly.
tools.usage:
PolynomialRemainder[p, q, x]
PolynomialRemainder[p, q, x, Modulus -> n]
tools.example:
PolynomialRemainder[x^3 - 1, x - 1, x]
PolynomialRemainder[x^3 + 2 x + 1, x^2 + 1, x]
PolynomialRemainder[p, q, x] === 0

tools.name: PolynomialGCD
tools.description: Gives the greatest common divisor of two or more polynomials, the highest-degree polynomial dividing all of them. Use it to find repeated roots (the GCD of a polynomial and its derivative) and to reduce rational expressions. Extension and Modulus options control the coefficient domain, and PolynomialLCM is the dual operation.
tools.usage:
PolynomialGCD[p1, p2, ...]
PolynomialGCD[p1, p2, Modulus -> n]
PolynomialGCD[p1, p2, Extension -> Automatic]
tools.example:
PolynomialGCD[x^2 - 1, x^2 + 2 x + 1]
PolynomialGCD[p, D[p, x]] /. p -> (x - 1)^2 (x + 3)
PolynomialLCM[x^2 - 1, x + 1]

tools.name: Resultant
tools.description: Gives the resultant of two polynomials with respect to a variable, which vanishes exactly when they have a common root. It is the classical tool for eliminating a variable from a pair of polynomial equations and for detecting shared factors. The result is a polynomial in the remaining variables.
tools.usage:
Resultant[poly1, poly2, var]
Resultant[poly1, poly2, var, Modulus -> p]
tools.example:
Resultant[x^2 - 1, x^2 + x, x]
Resultant[x^2 + y^2 - 1, x - y, x]
Resultant[p, D[p, x], x] /. p -> x^3 + a x + b
tools.notes: Resultant[p, D[p, x], x] is the discriminant up to a leading-coefficient factor; Discriminant computes it directly. Eliminate and GroebnerBasis handle larger systems.

tools.name: Discriminant
tools.description: Gives the discriminant of a polynomial in a variable, which is zero exactly when the polynomial has a repeated root. For a quadratic it reduces to the familiar b^2 - 4 a c. It is used to classify the nature of the roots without computing them.
tools.usage:
Discriminant[poly, var]
Discriminant[poly, var, Modulus -> p]
tools.example:
Discriminant[a x^2 + b x + c, x]
Discriminant[x^3 + p x + q, x]
Solve[Discriminant[x^2 + k x + 4, x] == 0, k]

tools.name: Numerator
tools.description: Gives the numerator of a rational expression, treating any factor with a negative power as part of the denominator. Apply Together first if the expression is a sum of fractions, otherwise the result may not be what you expect. It is the usual first step in converting a rational equation to a polynomial one.
tools.example:
Numerator[(x + 1)/(x - 1)]
Numerator[Together[1/x + 1/y]]
Numerator[a/b + c]
Solve[Numerator[Together[eqn]] == 0, x]

tools.name: Denominator
tools.description: Gives the denominator of a rational expression, collecting all factors raised to negative powers. Together with Numerator it splits a fraction into its two parts. Checking where the denominator vanishes is the standard way to find the poles of a rational function.
tools.example:
Denominator[(x + 1)/(x - 1)]
Denominator[Together[1/x + 1/y]]
Solve[Denominator[f] == 0, x]
Denominator[x^-2]

tools.name: PowerExpand
tools.description: Expands products and powers inside logarithms and roots, converting Log[a b] to Log[a] + Log[b] and Sqrt[x^2] to x. These transformations are not valid for all complex values, so PowerExpand deliberately ignores branch cuts and should be used only when the variables are known to be positive reals. A second argument restricts which symbols are treated this way.
tools.example:
PowerExpand[Log[a b]]
PowerExpand[Sqrt[x^2]]
PowerExpand[(a b)^n]
Simplify[Sqrt[x^2], x > 0]
tools.notes: Because PowerExpand can produce results that are wrong for negative or complex arguments, prefer Simplify with explicit assumptions where correctness matters.

tools.name: TrigExpand
tools.description: Expands trigonometric and hyperbolic functions of sums and multiple angles into products and powers of single-angle functions. It applies the addition and double-angle formulas systematically. Use it to break Sin[2 x] or Cos[a + b] into elementary pieces.
tools.example:
TrigExpand[Sin[2 x]]
TrigExpand[Cos[a + b]]
TrigExpand[Tan[x + y]]
TrigExpand[Sinh[2 x]]
tools.notes: TrigReduce is the inverse, rewriting products and powers as functions of multiple angles; TrigFactor factors trigonometric sums.

tools.name: TrigReduce
tools.description: Rewrites products and powers of trigonometric functions as a linear combination of functions of multiple angles, the inverse of TrigExpand. This is the canonical form for integration and for identifying frequency content. It works for hyperbolic functions too.
tools.example:
TrigReduce[Sin[x] Cos[x]]
TrigReduce[Cos[x]^2]
TrigReduce[Sin[x]^3]
Integrate[TrigReduce[Sin[x]^2 Cos[x]^2], x]

tools.name: TrigFactor
tools.description: Factors a sum of trigonometric functions into a product, applying sum-to-product identities. It is the trigonometric analogue of Factor and often reveals zeros of an expression. TrigFactorList returns the factors in structured {factor, exponent} form.
tools.example:
TrigFactor[Sin[x] + Sin[y]]
TrigFactor[1 + Cos[x]]
TrigFactor[Cos[a] - Cos[b]]
TrigFactorList[Sin[2 x]]

tools.name: TrigToExp
tools.description: Rewrites trigonometric, hyperbolic and inverse functions in terms of complex exponentials and logarithms. This often makes identities obvious that are hidden in trigonometric form, and it is a common preprocessing step before Simplify or Solve. ExpToTrig performs the reverse conversion.
tools.example:
TrigToExp[Sin[x]]
TrigToExp[Cos[x] + I Sin[x]]
TrigToExp[ArcTan[x]]
Simplify[TrigToExp[Tanh[x]]]

tools.name: ExpToTrig
tools.description: Converts exponentials with imaginary or real arguments back into trigonometric and hyperbolic functions. It is the inverse of TrigToExp and is used to present a result derived through complex exponentials in real trigonometric form. It also handles logarithms converting to inverse hyperbolic functions.
tools.example:
ExpToTrig[Exp[I x]]
ExpToTrig[(Exp[x] - Exp[-x])/2]
ExpToTrig[Log[x + Sqrt[x^2 + 1]]]
ExpToTrig[Simplify[TrigToExp[Sin[x]^2]]]

tools.name: ComplexExpand
tools.description: Expands an expression assuming all symbols are real, separating it into explicit real and imaginary parts. ComplexExpand[expr, {z1, ...}] instead treats the listed symbols as complex. The TargetFunctions option controls whether the answer is expressed with Re/Im, Abs/Arg or Conjugate.
tools.usage:
ComplexExpand[expr]
ComplexExpand[expr, {z1, z2, ...}]
ComplexExpand[expr, TargetFunctions -> {Re, Im}]
tools.example:
ComplexExpand[Re[(a + I b)^2]]
ComplexExpand[Abs[x + I y]]
ComplexExpand[Exp[I t]]
ComplexExpand[Sin[x + I y]]
tools.notes: Without ComplexExpand, Re and Im stay unevaluated for symbolic arguments because the kernel does not assume symbols are real.

tools.name: FunctionExpand
tools.description: Rewrites special functions and constants in terms of simpler or more explicit functions, for example expressing Gamma at half-integers with Sqrt[Pi] or Binomial with factorials. A second argument supplies assumptions. Use it when Simplify leaves an expression in terms of a special function that you know has an elementary form.
tools.example:
FunctionExpand[Gamma[5/2]]
FunctionExpand[Sin[Pi/12]]
FunctionExpand[BesselJ[3/2, x]]
FunctionExpand[Binomial[n, 2]]

tools.name: Refine
tools.description: Simplifies an expression using only the supplied assumptions, without the broad search that Simplify performs. It is fast and predictable, and is the right choice when you know exactly which fact needs to be applied. Refine[expr] uses the current setting of $Assumptions.
tools.example:
Refine[Abs[x], x > 0]
Refine[Sqrt[x^2], x < 0]
Refine[Sign[x], x > 0]
Refine[Log[Exp[x]], x \[Element] Reals]

tools.name: Assuming
tools.description: Evaluates an expression with additional assumptions in force, so that every Simplify, Refine, Integrate, Limit or Solve inside it sees them. It sets $Assumptions dynamically for the duration of the evaluation. This is the clean way to apply assumptions to a whole block of code instead of passing them to each call.
tools.example:
Assuming[x > 0, Simplify[Sqrt[x^2]]]
Assuming[n \[Element] Integers, Simplify[Sin[n Pi]]]
Assuming[a > 0, Integrate[Exp[-a x^2], {x, -Infinity, Infinity}]]
Assuming[Element[x, Reals], Refine[Conjugate[x]]]
tools.notes: Many functions also take an Assumptions option directly, which takes precedence over the assumptions set by Assuming.

tools.name: $Assumptions
tools.description: The global default assumptions used by Simplify, Refine, Integrate and other functions that accept an Assumptions option. Setting it makes the assumptions apply everywhere until it is reset, which is convenient in a notebook working on a single problem. Assuming sets it temporarily and safely.
tools.notes: Reset it to True to clear all global assumptions; forgetting to do so is a common source of confusing later results.

tools.name: Element
tools.description: Asserts or tests that an expression belongs to a domain such as Integers, Reals, Complexes, Rationals, Algebraics, Primes or Booleans, written infix with the \[Element] operator. It is the standard way to state assumptions about the type of a symbol. A list on the left asserts membership for several symbols at once.
tools.usage:
Element[x, dom]
x \[Element] dom
Element[{x, y}, dom]
tools.example:
Element[2, Integers]
Simplify[Sin[n Pi], Element[n, Integers]]
Assuming[Element[{x, y}, Reals], ComplexExpand[Abs[x + I y]]]
Reduce[Element[x, Integers] && x^2 < 10, x]
tools.notes: Element in an assumption position asserts membership; evaluated on explicit values it tests membership and returns True or False.

tools.name: Eliminate
tools.description: Eliminates variables from a system of simultaneous equations, returning the relations among the remaining variables. It is the algebraic way to derive a constraint that does not mention intermediate quantities, for example eliminating a parameter to get an implicit curve equation. It works with polynomial and rational equations.
tools.example:
Eliminate[{x + y == 5, x - y == 1}, y]
Eliminate[{x == Cos[t], y == Sin[t]}, t]
Eliminate[{a == r Cos[th], b == r Sin[th]}, th]
tools.notes: For larger polynomial systems GroebnerBasis with an elimination ordering is more controllable and often faster.

tools.name: GroebnerBasis
tools.description: Computes a Groebner basis for a set of polynomials, the canonical generating set of the ideal they define. With MonomialOrder -> EliminationOrder and a subset of variables it eliminates variables systematically, and it is the engine behind exact polynomial system solving. The CoefficientDomain and Modulus options choose the coefficient ring.
tools.usage:
GroebnerBasis[polys, vars]
GroebnerBasis[polys, vars, elimvars]
GroebnerBasis[polys, vars, MonomialOrder -> order]

parameters.name: Modulus
parameters.description: Prime modulus for computing over a finite field.

tools.example:
GroebnerBasis[{x^2 + y^2 - 1, x - y}, {x, y}]
GroebnerBasis[{x + y + z, x y + y z + z x, x y z - 1}, {x, y, z}]
GroebnerBasis[{x^2 + y, y^2 + x}, {x, y}, MonomialOrder -> Lexicographic]
tools.notes: Groebner basis computation can be extremely expensive in time and memory; try DegreeReverseLexicographic order first and eliminate variables only when needed.
